case_name: Wang v. British Columbia Medical Association
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Wang v. British Columbia Medical
Association,

2011 BCSC 1658

Date: 20111205

Docket:
S095777

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Caroline
Wang

Plaintiff

And

British
Columbia Medical Association (Canadian Medical Association - B.C. Division),
Geoffrey Marsden Appleton, Brian David Brodie, William (Bill) John Riddell
Cavers, Bradley Allen Fritz, Michael John Golbey, Nasirmohamed Jetha, Margaret
Anne MacDiarmid, John William (Bill) Mackie, Robin David Saunders, Mark David
Schonfeld, Barry John Turchen, John Michael Morris Turner, Geraldine Vance,
Carole Lynn Williams

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Hyslop

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

S.R.
Schachter, Q.C.

P.R.
Senkpiel

Counsel for the Defendants:

H.
Shapray, Q.C

A.Sabur

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

October
26 & 27, 2011

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

December
5, 2011

[
1
]

The plaintiff seeks in her amended notice of
application filed October 14, 2011, the following:

a.         Copies
of each Defendant’s Agendas and minutes (
in camera
or otherwise) for any
BCMA Board and Executive Committee Meetings held between June 2007 and October
2011, that have not already been produced;

b.         Tape
recordings (and transcripts, if they exist) of all of the BCMA Board and
Executive Committee Meetings held between June 8, 2008 and October 2011, that
have not already been produced;

...

e.         Copies
of any and all handwritten or electronic notes, including any notes made during
telephone conversations, or at meetings made between September 2005 and October
2011, and not otherwise included in (a);

f.          Copies
of any and all day timers, agendas, or calendars which would identify telephone
calls, conversations, or meetings relating to issues in the litigation, between
September 2005 and April 2008;

g.         Copies
of any and all electronic communications, including, but not limited to, any
Blackberry messaging messages, or messages from other similar electronic
devices, between September 2005 and October 2011;

h.         Copies
of all drafts of the President’s Letters/Bulletins dated February 2, 2008,
March 6, 2008, April 28, 2008, December 2, 2008, February 27, 2009, both hard
copy and electronic containing metadata, and any communications in relation
thereto;

i.          Copies of any and all
communications between the defendants and Ms. Murdoch (or any other external
counsel to the BCMA) from 2005 to April 2008 in relation to advice to the Board
regarding matters of governance, process or procedure, including, but not
limited to, communications relating to the process and procedure of the special
or “ad hoc” committee.

2.         An order that the Defendants:

a.         Provide
individual lists of documents;

b.         Provide
proper identification of privileged documents pursuant to Rule 7-1(7);

c.         Swear
and serve affidavits verifying their lists of documents pursuant to Rule
7-1(8);

d.         Provide the plaintiff with
digitized recordings of the September 2005 board meeting, the September 2007
board meeting, the November 2007 board meeting, and the June 2008 Annual
General Meeting, on the Plaintiff’s undertaking to pay such costs, if any, for
those recordings as may be ordered at a hearing before the registrar at the
conclusion of the litigation.

Background to Document Disclosure

[
2
]

The plaintiff brought an application for
production of further documents on May 19, 2010. This application was adjourned
generally after the defendants had delivered affidavit evidence in response and
a supplemental list of documents which was to satisfy requirements for
documents alleged to be material to the issues in the action.

[
3
]

On May 16, 2011, the plaintiff’s then counsel
took the position, that they needed tape recordings from meetings going back to
two years before the alleged defamation. A second notice of motion relating to
documents was filed May 24, 2010, and set for hearing on October 26 and 27,
2011.

[
4
]

The defendants produced a new list of documents
wherein they listed and produced all requested documents with the exception of
the post litigation audio recordings of the meetings of the board and executive
of the British Columbia Medical Association (Canadian Medical Association -
B.C. Division) (the “BCMA”), from June, 2008 to February 28, 2009.

[
5
]

In July of 2011, the plaintiff retained new
counsel. As a result, new counsel delivered to the defendants the amended
notice of application on October 17, 2011, which the defendants allege
“substantially broadened her demand for disclosure” (page 14 paragraph 40 of
the written argument of the defendants).

[
6
]

The plaintiff seeks document disclosure under
Rule 26 of the
Rules of Court
(the old rules). The defendants argue that
Rule 7-1 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
(the new rules) applies. In
response the plaintiff stated that it did not matter. I agree with the
defendants; the new rules apply.

[
7
]

This application was heard over a period of two
days. The plaintiff had not held any of their discoveries of the 15 defendants.
These discoveries are scheduled to take place in the months of November and
December of 2011. The trial is scheduled to take place starting January 23,
2012, for a period of 20 days. Both the plaintiff and the defendants are firm;
no adjournment is contemplated.

[
8
]

I agree with the plaintiff that in determining
whether documents are to be produced or not, is not based on the assessment of
the merits of the case, but rather on the pleadings. Nor, at this stage should
it be argued whether certain evidence or documents are admissible at trial. As
stated in the plaintiff’s reply, paragraph 7, “It is the document which may
tend to prove or disprove malice.”

[
9
]

The plaintiff’s position is that the defendants
were intent on punishing her after the 2005 referendum defeat and that the
defendants’ position is there was no such intent on their part. I agree with the
plaintiff’s statement that both parties have produced documents throughout this
time period, 2005 to 2008. It is not the time period that is important, but
whether all relevant documents have been produced.

[
10
]

Nor, should the date of the document determine
its production. It may be as the plaintiff points out in her reply, that the
defendants may have documents in which they discuss the plaintiff in defamatory
terms, or refer to alleged defamatory communications.

[
11
]

Further, this trial is not about whether the
manner in which the board governed the BCMA was right or wrong, or whether the
plaintiff was right or wrong in her criticisms of the board.

[
12
]

The defendants have identified in detail their
privileged documents and have made copies of certain board meeting agendas and
minutes for the years 2005, 2007 and 2008.

[
13
]

The defendants have also produced individual
lists of documents.

This Action

[
14
]

The plaintiff alleges that certain of the
defendants defamed her in written communications and in the case of one
defendant, verbal communications. The plaintiff alleges that those defendants
that did not specifically issue written or verbal communications are
responsible for the alleged defamation in that each of them did so by
“authorized, incited, assisted or encouraged the publication and distribution”
of the written and verbal communications.

[
15
]

The plaintiff pleads in the alternative, that
the BCMA is vicariously liable for the alleged defamation.

[
16
]

Similarly, the plaintiff alleges that the board
and the executive of the BCMA defamed the plaintiff as published by the
defendants, Saunders, Schonfeld and Vance, as did the president of the BCMA,
the defendant, Appleton in his publications.

[
17
]

The plaintiff alleges that the motive of the
defendants was to prevent her from her being re-elected to the board and her
continued involvement in medical politics.

[
18
]

The plaintiff also alleges there is a contract
between herself and the BCMA. The plaintiff alleges that the BCMA breached that
contract by not abiding by the requirements of utmost good faith, procedural
fairness and natural justice in all of their dealings with her and in all
aspects of the BCMA governance.

[
19
]

The plaintiff claims a number of heads of
damages. The plaintiff’s claims for special damages and all claims for economic
loss have been abandoned.

Background

[
20
]

The plaintiff is a medical doctor. She is a
member of the BCMA.

[
21
]

The BCMA has officers and delegates and a chief
executive officer (“CEO”). The CEO is the defendant, Dr. Mark David Schonfeld
(“Schonfeld”).

[
22
]

The plaintiff was elected as the voting member
of the board of directors of the BCMA representing district 8 in 1998. She was
elected thereafter to that position for five consecutive terms.

[
23
]

In May of 2007, the plaintiff was elected as
honorary secretary treasurer of the BCMA. This entitled the plaintiff to seek
two higher offices of the BCMA with the final office being that of the
president.

[
24
]

On May 21, 2008, the plaintiff was defeated in
the BCMA’s elections.

[
25
]

The responsibilities of the BCMA are detailed in
the defendants’ written argument in paragraphs 9 and 10. One of the
responsibilities of the BCMA is to negotiate the compensation the government
pays to non-specialist physicians. In 2005, the board of directors of the BCMA
recommended to the non-specialist physicians that they accept the government
proposal for their fees. The plaintiff was of the belief that the proposal was
flawed. As a result, she made her views known to the non-specialist physicians.
The proposal was required to be voted on by referendum of those entitled to
vote. The referendum to accept the government’s proposal was defeated.

[
26
]

The plaintiff’s theory is that “that the very
public and embarrassing defeat of the referendum earned her the enmity of the
defendants”. (Paragraph 12 of the argument of the plaintiff.)

[
27
]

The plaintiff claims to have been instrumental
at the 2006 annual meeting of the BCMA for the passing of certain resolutions
relating to openness and transparency to the operation of the BCMA. There was
conflict between the plaintiff and the board of directors of the BCMA as to
whether these resolutions were being implemented by the BCMA.

[
28
]

The conflict between the plaintiff, the
executive and the board continued and the various alleged defaming
communications came about which are contained in the consolidated notice of
civil claim (“CNCC”).

[
29
]

In 2006, the board of the BCMA passed and
revised a written code of conduct, further amended on April 13, 2007, which is
subject to modification, which the plaintiff agreed to abide by.

[
30
]

The defendants allege that by agreeing to the
code of conduct the plaintiff was obliged, after a decision was made by the
board to accept that decision and not undermine it. The defendants allege that
by the activities and pronouncements of the plaintiff, she failed to meet these
obligations. The defendants in the response to civil claim allege examples of
the plaintiff’s pronouncements and activities.

[
31
]

As a result, the BCMA board passed resolutions
deploring the actions of the plaintiff and that a committee be appointed to
investigate the allegations of breach of code of conduct of the plaintiff. The
committee was expanded to review not only the plaintiff’s conduct but also
“general issues of governance for the directors and officers of the BCMA as a
whole”. (Paragraph 28 response to civil claim.)

Law of Defamation

[
32
]

In order to defeat fair comment and qualified
privilege as pled by the defendants, the plaintiff must prove malice. Having
negative feelings or animosity towards a person, in this case the plaintiff, is
not sufficient to make a claim of defamation. It is much more. Raymond E.
Brown,
Brown on Defamation: Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand,
United States,
2d ed. (Toronto: Thomson Rueters Canada Limited,
1999), ch.
16
at 86 to 89:

Malice may be shown by evidence extrinsic to
the publication itself. In that regard, a court will look at the conduct of the
defendant throughout the course of events both before and after the defamatory
publication including his or her relationship with the plaintiff, personal
motivation, the emotional state in which the publication was made, any
repetition or republication of the same or comparable defamatory remarks, the
circumstances surrounding the investigation into or verification of the
accuracy of the charges, the conduct of the defense to the action, and whether
there has been a correction of charges that have later been found to be false.

(b) Conduct and Motivation of Defendant

...

An inference of
malice at the time of publication may be drawn from the state of mind of the
defendant on previous occasions. Therefore, a court will see whether there was
any previous business or social relationship between the parties which might
have affected the defendant’s actions, or whether they were complete strangers.
It will look to see if there is any evidence of personal animosity, antagonism,
enmity, feuding, friction, grudges, quarrels, rancor, threats, rivalry,
squables, strained relations, vindictiveness, hostility or bitterness between
the parties, or whether the defendant had previously waged a personal vendetta,
or harboured an ill feeling or grudge against, or had any differences with, the
plaintiff, or a group to which the plaintiff belonged, or whether he or she
belonged to a dissenting group within an organization, engaged in prior
altercations, litigation, or threats of litigation, exchanged heated or
defamatory words, or disseminated other untruths about the plaintiff.

[
33
]

In finding malice, the Supreme Court of Canada
stated in
Simpson v. Mair
,
2004 BCSC 754
:

81        In determining whether malice can
defeat fair comment, the law cautions that the court must be able to find that
malice was the dominant motive for the offending editorial.

82        The New Brunswick Court of Appeal
decision in Ross, supra at paras. 113-116, malice sufficient to undermine the
defence of fair comment was rejected, even though the defendant had admitted to
hating Ross' writing, had made "profane and denigrating" remarks
about Ross and had showed a very savage cartoon.

83        The court quoted with approval
from Brown, supra:

It is the
Defendant's primary or predominant motive in publishing the defamatory remark
that is determinative. 'Incidental gratification of personal feelings is
irrelevant." ... Dislike and ill will may be present but actual malice may
be entirely wanting. The fact that a defendant is annoyed, or dislikes the
plaintiff, or even contemptuous of him, and takes special delight in offending
or embarrassing him, and pleasure in the effect of the publication, or that he
was angry and rude, or indignant and resentful, and welcomed the opportunity to
expose him, will not defeat a privilege if it is otherwise exercised for a
proper purpose.

84        Having considered all the evidence
put forward in oral and written submissions on the issue of malice, although I
have not attempted to set out all of the arguments and evidence that was put
before the court, and having found that Mair was, in fact, actuated by malice,
I am unable to find that that this was his predominant or primary motive in
publishing the defamatory editorial. I consider that Mair was on a
"campaign" to expose what Mair believed were Simpson's
"irresponsible" statements and speeches against the teaching of
tolerance of a homosexual lifestyle in public schools. This, together with the
overall content of the defamatory editorial, is evidence supporting a finding
that the dominant motive for publishing the editorial was Mair's honestly held
opinion. That opinion was that the position taken by Simpson publicly in
support of a movement to resist the legitimizing of a homosexual lifestyle,
whether taught in schools or in relation to society in general, was a campaign
which he considered dangerous to values which he espoused. This was and is an
issue of public concern about which reasonable debate is important.

85        Thus,
the defence of fair comment cannot be defeated by the malice which I find
actuated the specific language used by Mair.

[
34
]

The defendants allege that not all extrinsic
evidence is relative to proving malice. Rather, it must be “so connected with
the state of mind of the defendant as to lead to the conclusion that he was
malicious at the date when the libel was published.” (
Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer
Pictures, Ltd.

(1950),
[1950] 1 All E.R. 449
HL (Eng.).)

[
35
]

As argued by the defendants:

Malice is a
state of mind. States of mind are facts which can be determined by a court only
b[y] inference. The author’s state of mind at a particular time may be of
assistance in making an inference about another state of mind which he held
soon afterwards. Per Blackburn J. in
Renouf v. Federal Capital Press of
Australia Pty. Ltd (1977),
17 A.C.T.R. 35 at 56 (S.C.).

Rule 7-1

[
36
]

Rule 7-1 has a different meaning than the old
rule, Rule 26. Mr. Justice Punnett in
Biehl v. Strang
,
2010 BCSC 1391
,
concluded the following:

10        Rule 7-1(1) is one of the more
controversial changes in the new Rules which came into force on July 1, 2010.
The rule states:

(1) Unless all
parties of record consent or the court otherwise orders, each party of record
to an action must, within 35 days after the end of the pleading period,

(a) prepare a
list of documents in Form 22 that lists

(i) all
documents that are or have been in the party's possession or control and that
could, if available, be used by any party of record at trial to prove or
disprove a material fact, and

(ii) all other
documents to which the party intends to refer at trial, and

(b) serve the list on all parties of
record.

11        Prior to July 1, 2010, Rule 26(1)
governed document production:

26(1) A party to
an action may deliver to any other party a demand in Form 92 for discovery of
the documents which are or have been in the party's possession or control
relating to any matter in question in the action, and the other party shall
comply with the demand within 21 days by delivering a list, in Form 93, of the
documents that are or have been in the party's possession or control relating
to every matter in question in the action.

...

14        The new rule replaces that
requirement. Now the initial production obligation is limited to what is
required to prove or disprove a material fact rather than what relates to every
matter in question. The assumption appears to be that in many, if not most
cases, such production will be sufficient. This change in scope is consistent
with Rule 1-3(2) which provides:

Proportionality

(2) Securing the
just, speedy and inexpensive determination of a proceeding on its merits
includes, so far as is practicable, conducting the proceeding in ways that are
proportionate to

(a) the amount
involved in the proceeding,

(b) the
importance of the issues in dispute, and

(c) the complexity of the proceeding.

15        Rule
7-1 (14) does provide for wider disclosure upon application to the court
including documents "relating to any or all matters in question in the
action".

[
37
]

In
Bieh
l, Punnett J. adopted the
definition of materiality found in Alan W. Bryant, Sidney N. Lederman &
Michelle K. Fuerst,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
, 3d ed. (Markham:
LexisNexis Canada, 2009) at para. 2.50:

The concept of
materiality, however, requires the court to focus on the material issues in
dispute in order to determine if the proffered evidence advances the party's case.

In other words, the requirement that the
disclosure relate to a material fact limits the breadth of what is relevant.

17        The authors of The Law of Evidence
in Canada define relevance at para 2.35:

S. 2.35 A
traditionally accepted definition of relevance is that in Sir J.F. Stephen's A
Digest of the Law of Evidence, where it is defined to mean:

... any two
facts to which it is applied are so related to each other that according to the
common course of events one either taken by itself or in connection with other
facts proves or renders probable the past, present, or future existence or
non-existence of the other.

Pratte J. in R.
v. Cloutier,
1979 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 709, accepted a definition from an early edition
of Cross on Evidence:

For one fact to be relevant to another,
there must be a connection or nexus between the two which makes it possible to
infer the existence of one from the existence of the other. One fact is not
relevant to another if it does not have real probative value with respect to
the latter.

[
38
]

Based on this analysis, I consider the
application of the plaintiff.

Documents Sought by the Plaintiff

[
39
]

The documents sought by the plaintiff are broken
down into the following categories:

1.

Defendants’ own minutes and agendas;

2.

Post litigation audio recordings;

3.

Notes, calendars and all electronic
communications;

4.

President’s draft letters;

5.

BCMA counsel communications re governance and
special committee.

[
40
]

In any event the plaintiff seeks that each
defendant verify their individual lists of documents pursuant to Rule 7-1(8).

Defendants’ Own Minutes, Agendas, and Notes, Calendars and
all Electronic Communications

[
41
]

The BCMA has already produced copies of the
agendas and minutes. The plaintiff argues that she took extensive hand written
notes at board meetings which have been produced. The plaintiff argues that
none of the defendants have produced such notes and that defamation cases “can turn
on the candid but damaging notes made by a defendant”. This, the plaintiff
argues, is an “extraordinary gap” in the production of each of the defendant’s
documents.

[
42
]

The plaintiff is seeking the individual
defendants’ agendas and minutes. She expects that these defendants may have
made notes on the agendas and the minutes relevant to this action.

[
43
]

The defendants argue that this would be
oppressive, wasteful and not probative of a material fact. The defendants argue
that the minutes and agendas have all been produced by the BCMA and that there
is no evidence that the defendants’ own copies “if retained have any unique
characteristics that would be probative to the matters at issue in the
litigation.” Further, that when the plaintiff is conducting the examination of
each defendant, they have any opportunity to ascertain whether such documents
exist.

[
44
]

Interestingly, in the plaintiff’s affidavit #1,
at paragraph 19 she stated that during her ten years as a member of the board,
and as a member of the executive committee:

...we were
encouraged by BCMA senior management to shred all of the materials that were
provided for our use during the meetings, including agendas and draft minutes.
A shredder was provided at the meetings for that very purpose. We were told
that the BCMA would maintain a complete set of these documents, which could be
referenced by Board/Executive Committee members whenever needed. As a result, I
did not feel the need to maintain a full set of all of the Board and Executive
Committee agendas, nor of the draft and final minutes of those meetings. In any
event, Board and Executive Committee Members were generally not provided with a
copy of minutes of meetings once they had been approved at a subsequent
meeting, and so I generally do not have complete copies of the approved minutes
of meetings.

[
45
]

In paragraph 20 of the plaintiff’s affidavit #1,
she states that she did not have a complete set of agendas or minutes of the
BCMA’s board and executive meetings and “it is impossible to identify specific
agenda items that are relevant. That is the very reason that I need to obtain
the complete copies of the agendas and the draft and final minutes that the
BCMA has refused to provide.”

[
46
]

Since producing these agendas and minutes to
February of 2009, the plaintiff has expanded her demand to 2011.

[
47
]

The defendants argue that the composition of the
board has changed over the years. There is nothing before the court to suggest
that the minutes and agendas contain additional communications that are not on
the agendas and minutes.

[
48
]

Cathy Cordell is in-house counsel for the BCMA.
In her affidavit #1, specifically addresses the contents of the meetings after
February 28, 2009. She specifically states that she has looked at the minutes
and agendas for the following meetings from June 8, 2008 through to February
28, 2009. She was present for all of those meetings, except for the meeting on
January 14, 2009. She swears that the contents of the meeting were entirely
unrelated to any of the matters that are at issue in this action and instead
relate to the affairs and ordinary business of the BCMA. She stated that the
plaintiff was only referred to
“on a very small number of occasions at the
Meetings, and in those instances in relation to her litigation and conflict
with the BCMA, its directors and staff”
(emphasis added).

[
49
]

I have concluded that the BCMA does not need to
produce further agendas and minutes of their meetings.

[
50
]

In the affidavit #5 of Amy J. Lewis, she
provides the following information relating to specific defendants:

1.         Appleton
is a former president of the BCMA. His practice is not to retain any documents
including emails, which he regularly deletes. He states that his home computer
systems/servers have been changed in the last two years and are “no longer
recoverable”. He states that any documents that he would have had, as it
relates to the issues in this lawsuit are to be found with the BCMA.

2.         Brodie
categorically denies keeping any agendas or minutes and that he has no email
communication correspondence pertaining to the matters at issue in this
litigation.

3.         Cavers
states that in May or June of 2009, his computer hard drive failed and he lost
all emails and documents that he had saved. As a result, there are no documents
in his possession or control that relate to the matters at issue.

4.         Fritz
states that he searched for documents that relate to the matters at issue and
was unable to locate any documents. He states that he does he does not keep old
emails “because his inbox gets overloaded and then incoming emails get
rejected”.

5.         Vance
states that she deletes all emails at the end of the day that have been
answered and she does this with respect to all topics. She categorically states
that she has no documents in her possession or control that relate to the
matters at issue in the litigation.

6.         Mackie,
Saunders, Turchen, Turner, and Williams have disclosed all documents and they
are not aware of any additional documents that are in their possession or
control relevant to this litigation at this time.

7.         MacDiarmid
states that after completing her service on the executive committee and the
board of directors, she disposed of all minutes and agendas, except those
emails which she has listed and produced. There are no other email
communications or other documents in her possession or control that are
relevant to the matters at issue in the litigation. This is the evidence before
the court.

8.         Mackie,
Saunders, Turchen, Turner and Williams have each “disclosed documents either in
Part 1 or in Part 3 (under the old rules) or Part 4 (under the new rules) in
Lists of Documents dated October 9, 2009 and/or October 21, 2011.”

9.         Mackie,
Saunders, Turchen, Turner, Williams and Jetha are not aware of any additional
documents in their “possession or control relevant to this litigation at this
time.”

[
51
]

The evidence before the court is that the
defendants have produced all their documents. The only areas that would be a
source of document disclosure are those emails that have been deleted or no
longer exist due to malfunctioning computers. This relates to the defendants
Appleton, Cavers, Fritz and Vance.

[
52
]

It may be determined by asking questions of some
of the defendants whether there were emails in which the plaintiff has been
referred to events or emails where events surrounding the alleged defamation
had been referred. If the answer is “yes”, then it can be determined whether
each defendant has attempted to recover those emails and what efforts they have
made to recover the emails. It may be that emails exist and that they can be
recovered. I will permit the plaintiff to renew this part of the application
before the case managing judge, seeking those emails if it is learned that the
emails can be recovered.

[
53
]

Based on the evidence that is before me I am
satisfied that the individual defendants have produced their documents. It is
certainly common at examinations for discovery, that the question of litigants’
documents are forgotten or not considered. I will permit the plaintiff to renew
this part of the application, requiring any defendant to produce such
documents. This can be done before the case managing judge.

Post Litigation Audio Recordings

[
54
]

The plaintiff demands all audio recordings of
the BCMA from June 8, 2008, to October, 2011. The defendants have produced
digitalized audio recordings of these meetings from June, 2007 to February,
2009 which have been listed and produced, despite the plaintiff now refusing to
pay for the cost of digitalizing and producing these audio recordings as
required by Rule 7-1(16). The defendants allege that the purpose of these
recordings is so accurate minutes of the meetings are produced. The plaintiff
disagrees with this. She claims that:

Historically,
the proceedings of the BCMA Board Meetings were recorded in order to have an
accurate record of the proceedings as a result of disputes over what had
transpired at contentious meetings that ended in litigation. Attached hereto as
Exhibit “B” is a true copy of any excerpt from the transcript of the February
1-2, 2008 BCMA Board Meeting in which the history and purpose of the tape
recording of Board Meetings is discussed.

I see no difference in either concept, both
are seeking accuracy.

[
55
]

The plaintiff argues that comments made after an
alleged defamation may be relevant to prove or disprove a material fact. The
defendants argue that these tapes are privileged. The plaintiff acknowledges
that anything related for the dominant purpose in seeking or giving legal
advice is privileged. However, the plaintiff argues that if there are any
personal comments made about the plaintiff, these are not privileged.

[
56
]

The plaintiff argues that the plaintiff’s name
was mentioned other than related to the litigation and that ought to be
produced. Ms. Cordell describes the minutes and agendas and the meetings and
listened to excerpts of audio recordings between June 8, 2008 and February 28,
2009. She swears

The vast
majority of the content of the Meetings is entirely unrelated to any of the
matters at issue in this action and instead pertains to the confidential
affairs and ordinary business of the BCMA.

She swears that
the plaintiff was only referred to in a small number of occasions at the
meetings. In those instances, it relates to:

...the dominant
purpose of the discussion relating to Dr. Wang or her litigation either
entailed seeking or giving of legal advice or was related to instructions to
counsel and/or the conduct, cost and strategy in respect of the litigation
related to Dr. Wang’s litigation, in all cases with the intention of being
privileged and confidential.

[
57
]

Ms. Cordell also swears that the BCMA was also
involved with litigation with insurance over the plaintiff’s claims.

[
58
]

As a result, based on this evidence, I conclude
that the plaintiff’s name arose between June of 2008 and February 28, 2009, in
discussions which are privileged and that the plaintiff’s name came up only in
that context.

[
59
]

The defendants seek that the BCMA disclose their
agendas, minutes and audio recordings for the period of February, 2009 to
October, 2011. Ms. Cordell swears that the demand for that period was so late,
that she was unable to locate them. She explained that the recordings are on an
analogue cassette tapes and for each individual meeting and there is “no
efficient way to review the relevant material”. She states that the BCMA has
not looked at any excerpts of these tapes. However, Ms. Cordell is able to
swear, based on her recollection in attending at these meetings (she was not
present at the July, 2009 meeting or the executive meetings of September 9 and
10 of 2011) that:

(a)        the vast majority of the
discussion had nothing to do with the Plaintiff or this litigation, but rather
pertained to the confidential affairs and ordinary business of the BCMA; and

(b)        to
the extent that the Plaintiff was brought up or discussed at all, it was for
the dominant purpose of seeking or obtaining legal advice, discussing legal costs
and strategies, or discussing issues [related] to the allegations in the
lawsuit. The communications were intended to be confidential and are
privileged.

[
60
]

The plaintiff criticizes Ms. Cordell for coming
to conclusions that the discussions were for the dominant purpose of litigation
and therefore privileged.

[
61
]

Comparing Ms. Cordell’s affidavit evidence in
paragraph 8 of her affidavit to that in paragraph 12 of her affidavit, it is
clear that Ms. Cordell is aware of what occurred at these meetings. She states
categorically, that the plaintiff’s name only came up as it relates to this
litigation. In paragraph 8 of her affidavit she sets out various privileged
communications that related not only to this litigation, but other litigation
in which the BCMA was involved.

[
62
]

I accept Ms. Cordell’s evidence as it relates to
the minutes, agendas and tapes from June 8, 2008 to those of October, 2011. I
will not order that the BCMA produce audio recordings of the minutes of the
board and executive meeting for that period of time.

Communications with Legal Counsel

[
63
]

The BCMA firstly claims privilege over pre
February, 2008, involving internal/external counsel of BCMA, involving matters
relating to governance, process, procedure and obligations of directors.
Secondly, the BCMA claims privilege over the drafts of president’s letters.
Thirdly, over the legal communications in relation to the special committee.

Pre - February, 2008

[
64
]

The plaintiff acknowledges in her pleadings that
starting in 2005 to February 2, 2008, she viewed herself as a participant in
the reform movement of the BCMA.

[
65
]

As a result, the plaintiff was often in conflict
with the board and executive committee. I have referred to the matter
pertaining to the referendum that was defeated. The plaintiff takes credit for
this defeat in her pleadings. (Paragraphs 30 to 34 of the CNCC).

[
66
]

At the BCMA’s annual meeting held in June of
2006, certain resolutions were passed. The plaintiff describes them as
transparency and openness in the conduct of the board and the executive
committee. The plaintiff is of the view that the board did not pursue these
resolutions that were passed in the annual general meeting in June of 2006.

[
67
]

It is alleged that in September of 2005, the
plaintiff was censured by the board. Following the meeting the president sought
an opinion from outside counsel, Jane Murdoch. Her opinion was made available
to the board, which would have included the plaintiff. No privilege is sought
for that communication. I note that there is a letter from Ms. Murdoch listed
in the plaintiff’s list of documents, whether this is an opinion or not, I
cannot be certain. The plaintiff argues that legal advice relating to
governance is not privileged. The BCMA says that it is privileged.

[
68
]

The BCMA argues that legal advice does not prove
or disprove a material fact that is - malice, or whether it is fair comment or
qualified privilege.

[
69
]

The BCMA alleges that the plaintiff is in
conflict with the board and is not entitled to the communications of the
board’s counsel, since she is not entitled to the solicitor/client privilege
that pass between the board and its counsel. As to the breach of contract claim
made by the plaintiff, it is not legal advice that determines whether the
plaintiff was entitled to procedural fairness and natural justice and whether
those implied contractual rights were breached. It is for the court to
determine whether the contract was breached.

[
70
]

The BCMA argues that the plaintiff is in
conflict with the board. The privilege is that of the BCMA, not the individual
members of the BCMA. In
Dublin v. Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto
,

2007 CanLII 8923 (ON SC)
, [2007] O.J. No. 1062, Perell J. at para. 62 says:

62
In
Re Livent Inc.
, in an
reductio ad absurdum

argument, Ground, J. points out that it would lead to a ludicrous result if a
director as litigant could negate his or her corporation's privilege in
precisely the circumstances when the privilege is necessary; namely, when the
corporation is seeking confidential legal advice about its legal relationship
with the particular director.

[
71
]

There is no doubt that the plaintiff was in
conflict with the board. In December of 2007, at a board meeting, the plaintiff
was cited for breach of the code of conduct. The plaintiff had already retained
counsel in December of 2007.

[
72
]

There was an alleged complaint which instigated
the striking of the special committee to investigate the plaintiff’s breach of
code of conduct. This is admitted by the plaintiff. The transcripts and audio
recordings of the board confirm this, and the terms of reference for striking
this special committee refer to the complaint.

[
73
]

The plaintiff commenced a petition in this court
seeking to dissolve the special committee and preventing the BCMA from pursuing
the goals of its special committee. The court found that at
Wang v. The
British Columbia Medical Association
,
2008 BCSC 1559
:

170      To
conclude, the special committee is not properly constituted to carry out a
review of any kind relative to Dr. Wang's conduct as a director. Even if the
special committee had been validly formed, Dr. Wang has demonstrated a
reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of both Drs. Golbey and Williams
such that they are disqualified. Consequently, the special committee ought to
be disbanded.

[
74
]

The Court of Appeal in
Wang v. The British
Columbia Medical Association
,
2010 BCCA 43
, among other conclusions stated:

73        Dr.
Wang's claim for breach of contract should not have been brought by petition.
Pursuant to Rule 2(3) it should not be struck for that reason alone, but the
pleadings and issues were not joined properly on that cause of action and it
was not presented to the Chambers judge as such. Her conclusions based on that
cause of action cannot stand.

[
75
]

The plaintiff argues that counsel for the BCMA
advised the court in April of 2010, Supreme Court petition, that it was “an
inquiry into her conduct and that of the directors in relation to the
governance of the Board”. The BCMA argues that at the time, the board sought
advice from counsel on process and procedure for the special committee. The
plaintiff was in conflict with the board in the sense that she had been cited
for breach of the code of conduct. She had retained counsel and there existed a
complaint that instigated the striking of the special committee to investigate
the plaintiff’s breach of the code of conduct. (Paragraph 79 of the written
argument of the defendants.)

[
76
]

The particular statement made by counsel at the
hearing of the petition in Supreme Court must be read with other statements
made at the same time. It was explained that the special committee was an
investigative body, not a discipline panel and that there was no charge. On the
facts, there was complaint.

[
77
]

I conclude that the BCMA had communication with
their counsel on the process and procedure of the special committee and any
opinions as to governance are privileged and they need not be disclosed.
Further, the legal advice received by the BCMA does not go to prove whether the
communications of the defendants are defamatory or whether the BCMA breached
its contract with the plaintiff.

President’s Draft Letters

[
78
]

The plaintiff is seeking draft letters of the
president, Appleton. These letters are dated February 2, 2008, March 6, 2008,
April 28, 2008, December 2, 2008 and February 27, 2009. Ms. Cordell in her
affidavit #1 states that no draft versions of the letter of March 6, 2008 have
been located by either her or Ms. Vance. Ms. Cordell states that the letters
described:

...were all
prepared or edited by the BCMA’s external counsel and reflect communications
between the BCMA and its counsel which entailed seeking or giving of legal
advice (directly or indirectly) and which was intended to be confidential.

[
79
]

The BCMA argues that Appleton’s draft
communications are privileged and contain or reflect legal advice given to him
and the BCMA by their counsel. The plaintiff argues that the defendants
Appleton, Schonfeld and Vance’s draft of their article and response to the
plaintiff’s article in the B.C. Medical Journal (“BCMJ”) was not produced when
the plaintiff’s draft was.

[
80
]

In the plaintiff’s CNCC (paragraph 20) she
complains of the words used by the defendants Appleton, Schonfeld and Vance in
an article in the BCMJ. The plaintiff’s amended notice of application does not
seek drafts of this article.

[
81
]

When preparing any drafts of the president’s
letters or bulletins, the evidence before the court is those communications
were all prepared or edited by the BCMA’s external counsel. I conclude that
those communications and any drafts of the president’s letters are privileged.

Day Timers, Calendars and Electronic Communications

[
82
]

The plaintiff alleges that notations in day
timers, calendars or electronic communications may give rise to meetings
between or among the individual defendants.

[
83
]

The plaintiff alleges as an example that there
are records of meetings between Appleton, Schonfeld and Saunders between
January 20, 2008 and February 1, 2008 which they allege “spawned the President’s
Letter of February 2”. (Paragraph 72 of the argument of the plaintiff.) The
plaintiff alleges a plot against her, and should be entitled to enquire into
this. (Paragraph 72 of the argument of the plaintiff.) The BCMA’s response is
this is speculation; that there is no plot.

[
84
]

I agree that just because a previous counsel of
the plaintiff did not ask for this information, does not mean it ought not to
be disclosed. The defendants argue that this demand is “too broad to be
meaningful” and is not linked to the proving or disproving of a material fact
and that the “documents demanded are not temporarily proximate to alleged
defamatory publications”. (Paragraph 49 of the written argument of the
defendants.)

[
85
]

It strikes me that at the examination for
discovery of the defendants, counsel for the plaintiff can ask if there were
any communications with or among the individual defendants (I am not referring
to communications with counsel) in which the plaintiff was discussed. At that
time, it can then be determined whether there were any documents (notations,
etc.) that arise, relating to that communication. If there are, I conclude that
they should have been referred to in the list of documents. The plaintiff is
then in a position of demanding that those documents be disclosed.

Should each of the Defendants be Required to Swear
Separate Affidavits Verifying their List Pursuant to Rule 7-1(8)

[
86
]

Both the plaintiff and the defendants placed
before me the law as it relates to this rule. The plaintiff and the defendants are
not in disagreement as to what the law is. I will not review it.

[
87
]

It would be unfair to the defendants to order
that they swear an affidavit verifying their documents. It was not until
October 17, 2011, that the breadth of the disclosure sought by the plaintiff
was made known to the defendants. The plaintiff’s action was stayed until
outstanding costs were paid. The deadline was September 6, 2011. On the last
day, the plaintiff paid the costs ordered. Further, had the examinations for
discovery of the defendants, taken place much earlier, this application may not
have been necessary. This delay I lay at the feet of the plaintiff (not
counsel).

[
88
]

It may be that as a result of the discoveries
conducted on each of the defendants, this application is warranted. At this
time, it is speculative, because at the time of hearing this application, no
discoveries of the defendants had taken place.

[
89
]

I adjourn the application for an affidavit of
each of the defendants verifying their list of documents. This application can
be brought on before the trial management judge if the plaintiff determines
that such an affidavit is required.

Costs

[
90
]

Although the defendants have been mainly
successful, the matter of documents seems unresolved until the completion of
the examination for discovery of the defendants or even perhaps the completion
of the trial. I order that the trial judge shall determine the costs of this
application.

SUMMARY

[
91
]

In summary:

1.         The
application for each individual defendant to produce additional documents is
dismissed. However, if it is found, after the examinations for discovery of
each individual defendant, that the documents do exist, then the plaintiff may
renew this part of their application before the case management judge.

2.         The
production of further documents, minutes, agendas and recordings of the
meetings is dismissed.

3.         Drafts
of the president’s letters and article are dismissed.

4.         The
plaintiff may, upon the individual defendants’ examinations for discovery being
completed, renew their application for documents that arise from communication
between or among the defendants in the nature of calendars and all electronic
communications.

5.         The
trial judge shall determine the costs of this application.
